summary: Proposes a Telnet option that lets the serving host control when characters typed by a user are echoed and when they are sent. The aim is to cut down the number of network messages that character-at-a-time typing with remote echo would otherwise need.

plainLanguage.summary: The RCTE Telnet option lets a serving host control when the user's host displays typed text and sends it over the network. Grouping characters into larger units can reduce network traffic compared with sending and echoing each character separately.

subtitle: A Telnet option for controlling echo and grouping terminal input before transmission.

tldr.problem: Character-at-a-time typing with remote echo could require four network messages for each character.
tldr.mechanism: RCTE lets the serving host tell the using host when to echo text and which characters trigger transmission of buffered input.
tldr.outcome: The authors estimate that grouping input and reducing echo could cut character-mode terminal traffic by almost 90 percent. RFC 560 was updated by RFC 581.

today: RFC 560 is listed as Unknown and was updated by RFC 581. The text does not state whether the option was deployed.

sections.title: Reducing Echo Traffic
sections.content:
With character-at-a-time transmission and echo from the foreign host, each typed character causes four network messages: the character, its RFNM, the echoed character and its RFNM. The RFC estimates that removing most echoing and grouping characters into useful units could reduce interactive terminal traffic by almost 90 percent.

The option is intended for full-duplex hosts. The RFC says the existing Go-Ahead feature is sufficient for half-duplex servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending each typed character and waiting for its remote echo creates many network messages. RCTE aims to reduce them by sending groups of characters and limiting remote echo.

sections.title: Negotiating RCTE
sections.content:
The option is called Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing (RCTE). Telnet commands negotiate whether the hosts will use it. The default is WON'T RCTE and DON'T RCTE, meaning neither host controls the other's terminal printer.

After agreement, the using host acts on commands from the serving host. It initially holds echo printing until directed otherwise. The serving host sends RCTE subcommands to control printing and the handling of typed input.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts must agree to use RCTE. Once they do, the user's host follows the serving host's instructions about displaying and sending input.

sections.title: Break and Transmission Characters
sections.content:
An RCTE subcommand contains a command byte and may include bytes describing Break and Transmission character classes. A Transmission character requires the using host to send the text collected so far. A Break character also ends the current echo or discard action until another command arrives.

The command can say whether to echo the text and the Break character, keep existing classes or replace them. When RCTE starts, no Transmission classes are active; Break classes 4, 5 and 9 are active. Telnet commands always act as Break characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The serving host defines which typed characters end a group and trigger a send. A Break character also pauses the current display rule until the next instruction.

sections.title: Session Flow and Limits
sections.content:
The using host buffers input until a Transmission or Break character occurs, and echoes or suppresses the input according to the latest RCTE command. Output from the serving host is printed immediately and must end with an RCTE command. Any new server output returns control to the initial echo-waiting step.

The RFC's example shows a password being sent without echo. It also warns that input buffering may overflow, especially on TIPs, and that the option's overhead is not justified for true character-at-a-time use.
sections.plainLanguage: The using host collects input and follows the latest echo instructions. The RFC's example hides a password, and it warns that a full input buffer can cause characters to be lost.

items.label: Print through Break
items.desc: Echo text up to and including the Break character.

items.label: Skip Break
items.desc: Echo text up to the Break character, but do not echo the Break character.

items.label: Skip text
items.desc: Do not echo text up to the Break character, but echo the Break character.

items.label: Skip through Break
items.desc: Do not echo text or the Break character.
